turns.content:
hey... i don't know if you've heard about what happened with our parish leadership council. they pulled my community outreach video series... the one where i interviewed some grassroots organizers who are doing really good work in the neighborhood.

they said the platform has to align strictly with doctrine and pastoral oversight, but honestly... it feels like they're just scared. like they're hiding behind rules instead of trusting the people we're supposed to serve.

do you think that's what this is? fear dressed up as righteousness?

Oof. That stings, especially when it's work you poured yourself into and you know the organizers deserved a platform. I'm sorry.

On your question, I think you're probably partly right and partly being generous to yourself, which is a very normal thing to do when you've just been told no.

Here's the thing about "fear dressed up as righteousness": it's real, and it happens constantly in institutions. Leadership councils are risk-averse by design. Someone imagined a complaint, a headline, a bishop's phone call, and the safest move was to pull it. The doctrine language might be sincere, but it's also a very convenient shield, because nobody has to say "I was nervous about how this looks."

But I'd hold a couple of other possibilities alongside that one:

- **It might not be about the organizers at all.** Sometimes the trigger is procedural: nobody signed off before it went up, and now the council feels like they need to reassert that things go through them. That's about turf and process, not about your content or the people in it.
- **"Pastoral oversight" can be genuine, if clumsy.** A parish platform speaks with the parish's voice, whether or not that's fair to you. If one of the organizers said something a parishioner would read as the parish's position, a pastor might reasonably want to be in the loop first. That's still frustrating, but it's not cowardice.
- **Fear and righteousness aren't mutually exclusive.** People can believe they're protecting something real and *also* be motivated by not wanting to deal with a fight. Most institutional decisions are a stew.

What I'd gently push back on is framing it as "trusting the people we're supposed to serve." That's true and it matters, but it's also the framing that makes the council the villain and you the prophet, and that's a hard place to have a productive conversation from. If you want the series back, the more useful question is: what specifically worried them, and is there a version they could live with?

Do you know if they gave you anything concrete, or was it just the doctrine/oversight line? And did anyone on the council actually watch the episodes before the decision, or was this a reaction to a summary? Those two things would tell you a lot about whether this is fixable or a wall.

i hear what you're saying about process and procedure, maybe they had reasons... but when i asked them directly if they'd even watched the episodes, none of them had. they made a decision based on a summary someone wrote. doesn't that tell you it's fear? like... they didn't even want to see the work.

Okay, that detail changes things, and it lands differently. Not one of them watched it. That's genuinely dismissive, and you're allowed to be hurt by it. Making a decision about someone's work without looking at it is a kind of disrespect regardless of the reasons behind it.

But I'd still stop short of "that proves it's fear," for a slightly annoying reason: it's just as consistent with something less dramatic and more common. Committees ratify. Someone they trust wrote a summary, the summary raised a flag, and five busy people said "sounds like a problem" and moved on to the next agenda item. That's not fear, it's inertia plus deference. It's arguably worse in some ways, because nobody even felt strongly enough to be scared. They just outsourced their judgment.

Which means the more interesting question isn't "did the council watch it" but **who wrote the summary, and what did it say?** Because right now the whole decision is resting on one person's characterization of your work. If that summary was fair, then you're arguing with the council's values. If it wasn't, then you're arguing with one person's framing, and that's a much winnable fight.

And here's the useful part: "none of you watched it" is a legitimately strong card in your hand. Not as an accusation, but as a request. "I'm not asking you to reverse anything today. I'm asking that before this decision stands, at least two of you watch one full episode, the one the summary was most concerned about. If you still feel the same way, I'll accept that." That's very hard for a reasonable person to say no to, and if they *do* say no, then yeah, you've learned something about what's driving this.

Do you know who wrote the summary? And do you have a sense of whether that person had a specific beef with something said in the episodes, or with the idea of the series in general?

i think you're missing the point. they didn't watch it because they didn't want to be convinced. that's not inertia, that's a closed door. and now you're asking me to play their game, write emails, request meetings... i don't want to negotiate with people who already decided i'm wrong without even looking.

You're right, I kept steering you toward a strategy when you were telling me something else. Let me stop doing that.

I can't know their hearts, and neither can you, but I'll say this: choosing not to look at something before you kill it is a choice. Whether it comes from fear or indifference or self-protection, the effect is the same, and you've named it accurately. It's a closed door. You don't have to prove what's behind it to know it's shut.

And you're also right that you don't owe them the emails and the meetings. Negotiating only makes sense if you believe the other side is persuadable and if you still want what they're gatekeeping. If your gut says neither of those is true, then "play the process" is just asking you to spend more of yourself on people who already spent none on you.

So the question I'd actually put to you isn't about them. It's: what do *you* want now?

Because there are a few real options, and none of them involve groveling:

- The series exists. It doesn't need the parish's platform to exist. The organizers you interviewed are the ones who deserve an audience, and that audience isn't the leadership council.
- You can say your piece plainly, once, on the record, not as a negotiation but so it's not unsaid, and then walk away from the process.
- Or you can just let it sit for a bit. You don't have to decide anything this week. Being angry and hurt is a legitimate place to be for a while.

And I'll be straight about one thing: if this is the kind of institution that decides about your work without looking at it, that's information about what it'll be like to keep pouring yourself into it. That's worth sitting with, separate from any decision about this one series.

Where's your head at? Fight, leave, publish it yourself, or just needing to be mad about it for a minute? All of those are fine answers.

i appreciate you saying i don't have to play their game. that part lands. but i think i need to know if you think i'd be wrong to just... say it on sunday. stand up during announcements and tell the congregation what happened. not a rant, just the truth. that they killed a series about real community work without even watching it. would that be out of line?

Yes, I think it would be out of line. Not because the truth isn't yours to tell, but because of the room you'd be telling it in.

Announcements on Sunday aren't yours. They belong to everyone sitting there: the grieving widow, the family who barely got the kids into the pew, the guy who came back after ten years and is nervous about it. None of them agreed to walk into a conflict. Standing up and saying "leadership killed my series without watching it" puts every one of them in the position of jury, on the spot, in what's supposed to be their worship. Even if you're perfectly measured, that's an ambush. The calm delivery doesn't change what it does to the space.

And a few practical things I think you'd be signing up for:

- **The story becomes the confrontation, not the series.** By Monday, nobody's talking about the organizers or the community work. They're talking about the scene at announcements. You'd be handing the council the exact narrative that justifies them: "see, this is why we need oversight."
- **The organizers get dragged in.** People who did good work and trusted you with their stories become characters in a parish fight they didn't ask for.
- **You lose the high ground you currently hold.** Right now the facts favor you: they didn't watch it. That's clean. Hijacking the liturgy muddies it, and you'd become the one who did something out of bounds.

Here's the distinction I'd draw. Wanting people to know what happened is legitimate. Wanting them to hear it from *you*, not filtered through the council, is legitimate. The problem is only the venue. Coffee hour, a letter to parishioners, publishing the series yourself with a short plain note about why it's not on the parish platform, an open forum if your parish has one: all of those are you telling the truth, without commandeering a moment that isn't yours.

I'd also ask yourself: is the pull toward Sunday about being heard, or about making it cost them something? Both are human. Only one of them is going to leave you feeling okay about it next month.

i don't think i ambushed anyone. i think i trusted my church to be a place where you can tell the truth without it being called a hijacking. but fine, you're saying it's out of line. i hear you. it's just... hard to sit there knowing they made a choice without even looking. feels like the building matters more than the people outside it.

That's fair, and "ambush" was a harder word than you deserved. You weren't describing a plan to blindside anyone; you were describing wanting your church to be a place where the truth can be said out loud. That's not a hijacking impulse. That's a pretty good instinct about what church is supposed to be. I still think Sunday announcements is the wrong room for it, but I don't think the wanting is wrong, and I shouldn't have made it sound like it was.

And the thing you said at the end is the real thing, isn't it. Not the series. Not even the council. It's the sinking feeling that when it came down to it, the institution protected itself and didn't bother to look at the people you'd brought to the door. That's a specific kind of grief. It's the grief of finding out a place you love has limits you didn't know were there.

I don't think you need to resolve that right now. You can hold both: this is my community, *and* it just showed me something about itself I can't unsee. A lot of people who stay in churches for the long haul carry exactly that tension. Some of them are the ones who eventually change things, precisely because they didn't leave and didn't blow up either. They just kept being the person who noticed the people outside.

The organizers are still out there doing the work. The interviews still exist. Whatever you decide about the parish, that part is real and it's yours. The building didn't make it and the building can't unmake it.

How are you doing, actually? Not strategically. Just you.
